questions.question: What are generics in TypeScript and when do you use them?
questions.title: Typescript Generics
questions.direct_answer: Generics are type parameters — placeholders for types filled in per-use, like function parameters but for types. `<T>(value: T): T` means 'whatever type you give me, you get back the same type.' Use them when a function/type works identically across multiple types: identity helpers, containers (Array<T>, Map<K,V>), API wrappers (fetchJson<T>(url): Promise<T>), and utility types (Partial, Pick). They preserve the input-output type relationship that any/unknown would erase.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The variance intuition (what <T> really does): a generic is a type-level function from types to types. The compiler SPECIALIZES it per call site: first([7,8,9]) instantiates T = number and type-checks that specialization. Unlike any (one type that stands for everything, losing all checking), each instantiation keeps full type-safety for its specific T.

The generic ecosystem you already use (the connection to daily code): Array<T>, Map<K,V>, Promise<T>, and the utility types — Partial<T> (all fields optional), Required<T>, Pick<T, K> (subset of fields), Omit<T, K> (fields minus K), Record<K, V> (typed map), ReturnType<T> (a function's return type). These are library generics + mapped types — understanding them is understanding generics' real payoff: writing reusable typed building blocks.

The advanced forms (senior-level recognition): default type parameters (<T = string>), conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y — type-level branching used by Extract/Exclude), mapped types ({[K in keyof T]: ...} — transforms every property, the machinery of Partial), and const type parameters (<const T> for literal inference). The honest guidance: these power library and framework types; application code mostly needs constraints + the utility types + occasional inference — reaching for conditional types in app code is usually over-engineering.
